svg.title: How an EIGRP query spreads when there is no feasible successor, and the four ways to bound it
svg.desc: A topology on the left shows a failed link at the edge, a query fanning out hop by hop because no router along the path holds a feasible successor, and the stuck-in-active timer at three minutes after which the adjacency is torn down and rebuilt. A timeline on the right shows the four phases: the link fails, the router goes active and queries all remaining neighbours, each neighbour that also lacks a feasible successor propagates the query, and after three minutes without a reply the neighbour relationship is reset, which makes the outage much larger than the original link failure. Four bounding tools are listed: stub routing so the branch never receives queries; summarization so a query is answered at the boundary rather than propagating; query filtering with distribute lists; and a clear rule about which routers may be transit. The closing note says the design objective is not faster queries but fewer of them.
svg.text: With no feasible successor, one dead link becomes a network-wide question
The design goal is not faster queries. It is fewer of them, and shorter distances for the ones that happen
THE QUERY FAN-OUT
Edge-1
Dist-1
Core-1
Core-2
Branch-7
link down
1. The link fails; the router runs out of successors and goes active.
2. It queries every remaining neighbour.
3. Each neighbour with no feasible successor propagates the query.
4. Every one of them waits, holding routes in active state.
5. No reply within 3 minutes → adjacency reset. Routes that
were never in question disappear. The outage is now much
larger than the link that actually failed.
The mechanism is bounded by the topology, not by the timer.
FOUR WAYS TO BOUND THE QUERY DOMAIN
1. Stub routing
The branch announces its own prefixes and never receives queries. Use it on every leaf site.
2. Summarization
A query for a prefix inside the summary is answered at the boundary, and stops there.
3. Query filtering
A distribute list decides which queries may pass. Effective, but it must be documented.
4. A transit rule
Write down which routers may be transit for which prefixes, and configure the rest as stubs.
The failure mode this chapter exists to prevent: 200 branches, none configured as stub, no summarization at the aggregation layer.
One access switch reboots, one query has no feasible successor, and the query reaches every branch. For three minutes, routes across the
whole network sit in active state. When people describe “the network goes down when any site restarts”, this is the mechanism.
Design rule to write into the document: a distance-vector protocol is only as scalable as its query boundaries. Draw the query domain on the same
diagram as the addressing plan, because it is the same boundary. Stub at the leaves, summarization at the aggregation layer, and no route that
depends on a query travelling more than one hop.
Verification: shut an interface on a branch, and count how many routers enter active state. The number should be one. If it is not, the query domain was never designed.
